scenes.name: Beat, R&B y mod pop británico
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Tras el éxito de los Beatles, las cuatro grandes discográficas (EMI, Decca, Pye y Philips) saquearon metódicamente las provincias: firmaban barato y esperaban a ver qué pegaba. Pye, del veterano Louis Benjamin, tenía a los Kinks y a los Searchers y fama de contratos miserables. Los Ugly’s de Birmingham, nacidos del skiffle y curtidos en los clubes alemanes, se distinguían por su conciencia social; la cara B de su tercer single, «A Quiet Explosion» (21 de enero de 1966), con órgano Vox Continental, un riff con eco a lo Delia Derbyshire y un bajo descendente que es la bomba cayendo, desapareció en la sobreproducción del momento, pero es un disco extraño y auténtico que se acerca a la psicodelia. A principios de 1966 las bases del beat y del R&B se llevaron al límite, como bajo una enorme presión: «Keep on Running» de Spencer Davis casa soul y mod pop, los Wheels de Belfast aceleran sin freno en «Bad Little Woman» y los Poets de Glasgow, de Andrew Loog Oldham, desquician el «Baby Don’t You Do It» de Marvin Gaye.

scenes.name: The Rolling Stones
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Andrew Loog Oldham, su Svengali adolescente, los moldeó como los anti-Beatles: groseros y divisivos, «monstruos melenudos del Id adolescente» (tras la multa por orinar contra el muro de un garaje en 1965, puso a Jagger en el titular). En 1965 «(I Can’t Get No) Satisfaction», con su fuzz y su racimo final de «no», expresó una insatisfacción casi cósmica con el consumismo que los había encumbrado; Jagger, culto y elocuente en Charlie Is My Darling de Peter Whitehead, decía que el pop por fin hablaba de levantarse, ir a trabajar y sentirse jodido. «19th Nervous Breakdown» (4 de febrero de 1966), grabado en Los Ángeles al final de una gira de cuarenta fechas, fue la primera gran declaración pop del año: dos guitarras metálicas entrelazadas (Richards y Brian Jones por última vez en un single), ritmo rockabilly maníaco, casi cuatro minutos sobre una pobre niña rica sin salida. Cada single debía superar al anterior en doce semanas. Mientras se codeaban con Anita Pallenberg, Robert Fraser o Christopher Gibbs, Aftermath (abril), entero de composiciones propias, fue el LP del año, aunque en «Stupid Girl» o «Under My Thumb» el desprecio por las mujeres no inquietó a nadie.

podcast.title: Composer of Key Sample, No Remuneration
podcast.body: Despite being the original composer of the "cinco famos anotas" (five famous notes) that formed the core instrumental sample in "Bitter Sweet Symphony," Andrew Loog Oldham ultimately did not receive any financial compensation for their use after the complex legal battles concluded. This situation left him feeling deeply frustrated regarding the outcome. "Alando Conban en el fondo ha sido el compositor de esas cinco famos anotas no veo un duro y el pobre también lo ve muy frustro ante el grupo de ver pues yo es podéis imaginar cómo quedarlo."

podcast.title: Loss of Rights to Instrumental Versions
podcast.body: Andrew Loog Oldham had previously been sued by Allen Klein over the rights to the instrumental versions of The Rolling Stones' songs he had created in the late 1960s. As a result of this earlier legal dispute, Oldham lost all rights he held over these instrumental tracks, which subsequently fell under Allen Klein's ownership. "Alinclain ya en su día habían mandado a Alinclain por los derechos de estas versiones instrumentales que había hecho a finales de los 60 y por el cual había acabado perdiendo todos los derechos que tenía suelas canciones."

podcast.title: Producer and First Manager of The Rolling Stones
podcast.body: Andrew Loog Oldham held significant roles with The Rolling Stones, serving as their first professional manager and also as their producer. This professional relationship places him in a key position regarding the origins of the music later sampled by The Verve. "Alan Luke, aparte de grabar estas versiones sinfónicas, fue el primer banal de que tuvieron los Rolling Stones profesional. Era el más de manal y era el productor del grupo."

podcast.title: Producer and First Manager of The Rolling Stones
podcast.body: Andrew Loog Oldham was the manager of The Rolling Stones during their early career, releasing "The Rolling Stones Songbook" in 1966 which contained the orchestral arrangement of "The Last Time" later sampled by The Verve. He was later succeeded by Allan Klein. "Andrew Lou Geoldem, the manager of the Rolling Stones back in the day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Symphonic Versions of Rolling Stones Songs
podcast.body: Andrew Loog Oldham was responsible for creating symphonic versions of Rolling Stones songs in the late 1960s. One of these instrumental versions, specifically featuring five repetitive notes from "The Last Time," was later sampled by The Verve for their song "Bitter Sweet Symphony." Oldham initially granted permission for its use, but he subsequently filed a lawsuit, feeling he deserved more prominence than agreed upon as the song became hugely successful, although his initial demand did not succeed. "Esa rifa, al finalmente, pertenecía a una grabación de finales de los 60 de Alan Luke que hacía versiones sinfónicas de Rolling Stones."

podcast.title: University Lecturer
podcast.body: Andrew Loog Oldham, who was the very first manager of The Rolling Stones, is currently teaching a university course in Camloops. "The very first manager the Rolling Stones ever had is now teaching a university course in Camloops."

xref.title: Arranger of "The Last Time" String Figure
xref.body: David Whitaker was the orchestrator hired to arrange the string figure in the 1966 Andrew Loog Oldham Orchestra's version of The Rolling Stones' "The Last Time." This six-second string figure, which he composed and arranged, became central to The Verve's "Bittersweet Symphony" lawsuit. Despite his pivotal role in creating the sampled material, he received no additional compensation beyond his initial fee in 1966. "They were written and arranged by an orchestrator for higher guy named David Whitaker."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Copyright Dispute and Loss of Publishing Rights
xref.body: The Verve faced a significant legal battle over their song "Bittersweet Symphony," stemming from a licensed sample. Despite an initial agreement for 50% of earnings, Abkco Music (controlled by Allen Klein) and Andrew Loog Oldham sued, leading to The Verve being forced to surrender 100% of the song's publishing rights, resulting in Mick Jagger and Keith Richards being credited as co-writers and receiving all royalties. "Alright, give us 100% of the money made from this song or we will force you to recall every single copy of the song an album from every store and radio station and whatever worldwide."

xref.title: Lawsuit for Royalties
xref.body: Andrew Loog Oldham, who was the original manager of The Rolling Stones, sued The Verve, claiming they owed him $1.7 million in royalties for "Bittersweet Symphony" due to the use of a five-note progression from his orchestra's version of "The Last Time." "Lugoldem figured he was owed $1.7 million."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Orchestral Interpretations for Easy Listening
xref.body: The Andrew Loog Oldham Orchestra created orchestral versions of The Rolling Stones' songs, released in 1965. These arrangements were designed to be "watered down" for fans of easy listening music, catering to those who might be offended by the original rock and roll sound. "I mean, really water them down so people who were offended by rock and roll wouldn't be offended by these rock and roll songs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Originator of "Bittersweet Symphony" Snippet
xref.body: David Whitaker was the orchestral arranger who originally wrote the distinctive five-note progression in Andrew Loog Oldham's version of "The Last Time." This specific musical phrase later served as the inspiration and sampled basis for The Verve's "Bittersweet Symphony." "He wrote that five note bit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
